title: Repeatable services: Organisational redesign changes legal delivery
desc: Compares incumbents, AI-native providers and in-house teams while pricing, buyer value and partnership incentives remain unsettled.

kps.k: The central proposition is organisational redesign: AI could turn legal expertise into repeatable services rather than merely accelerate individual lawyers.
kps.d: Harvey’s founders and Legora’s Max Junestrand envisage encoding firm knowledge, client context and working methods into specialised systems that scale beyond associate headcount. AI-native providers describe building delivery around that premise: Covenant offers client-facing software, Norm Law integrates AI into the first pass, and Crosby combines practising lawyers with engineers. These approaches differ from adding a copilot to existing work. Their shared commercial claim is that firms can sell expertise and completed services through new operating models; technology-like scale and margins remain conditional expectations, not established industry outcomes.

qs.q: Instead of only being to work with my pyramid of associates, I'm a I'm now able to do work that I could scale to, you know, hundreds or thousands of clients at the same time.
qs.a: AI Driven Legal Evolution - Max Junestrand - Legora - Episode #64 · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: Um what we're doing here and what we have here is kind of first pass AI at the premise, true AI nativity.
qs.a: AI First Firms Joining the AmLaw 100 is 'Inevitable' — Batya Nadler (Partner, Norm Law) on Legally Disrupted ep. 55 · AI-native providers · 2026

kps.k: The strategic divide concerns who should deliver the work: software-enabled incumbents, integrated AI-native providers or stronger in-house teams.
kps.d: Junestrand prefers supplying software to existing lawyers rather than owning both software and legal-service delivery. Pereyra identifies the operational burden of building two businesses, drawing on interviews with former Atrium personnel. Crosby takes the opposite approach, arguing that ownership of delivery enables close lawyer–engineer feedback and deeper automation. Lawhive presents aggregation around proprietary AI as a way for smaller consumer firms to obtain capabilities they cannot fund individually. These are competing organisational theories, not comparative evidence that one structure performs better. Harvey and Legora remain software vendors in these accounts, distinct from providers delivering legal work.

qs.q: Don't think that owning the entire  service layer and software layer is a winning strategy.
qs.a: Legora CEO, Max Junestrand: $7M ARR in a Day | Harvey vs Legora: Is a Legal AI Winner Takes All? · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: But when we dug more into it, the big challenge that they ran into was you're essentially just building two different companies, right?
qs.a: Gabe Pereyra — Harvey (No Priors Ep. 142) · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: Corporate buyers shift the test from software adoption to the incremental value of outside counsel.
kps.d: Ford’s Darth Vaughn prioritises actionable decisions, risk assessment and proactive problem-solving over document production. Moderna’s Shannon Thyme Klinger reports preparing sophisticated first drafts internally and commissioning narrower outside review. Eudia and Wordsmith frame their opportunity around insourcing, integrated knowledge and reduced external spending; McNairn’s prediction that most departments will halve external spending by the end of 2027 remains a forecast. The LawTech Talks discussion adds selective allocation between firms, in-house teams and ALSPs such as Axiom, with shared analysis reducing duplication. Yet Nadler and the Eudia discussion stress that clients may still lack the people, expertise or time needed to implement automation themselves.

qs.q: We do many more first drafts now even of sophisticated licensing agreements and then send them to our outside deal council and say can you please spend an hour on this and can you look at the following provisions that has been fantastic from an efficiency and cost savings perspective.
qs.a: Shannon Thyme Klinger — Moderna (Chief Legal Officer) on rewiring a legal function around AI · In-house counsel · 2025

qs.q: And [snorts] I think the net of those three forces will mean that by the end of 27, I think you'll see the majority of in-house teams sort of slash their external spend by at least half.
qs.a: Ross McNairn — Wordsmith.ai (in-house legal orchestration) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Pricing may diversify without eliminating the billable hour, and efficiency does not guarantee lower prices or higher margins.
kps.d: General Legal describes flat-rate delivery; Crosby bills by document; Soxton gives an approximately $100-per-contract example with lawyer review. Weinberg predicts fixed fees for AI-assisted tasks alongside hourly, potentially more expensive specialist advice. Crosby also preserves hourly billing for sophisticated work whose scope is difficult to predict. Under fixed fees, efficiency can improve margins, but providers must price negotiation rounds, human work and inference costs. Daniels rejects loss-leading price competition based on hoped-for model improvements, preferring speed and quality. Junestrand and Weinberg separately argue that automating discounted routine services can preserve relationships that lead to larger mandates; they supply commercial reasoning rather than measured retention gains.

qs.q: guessed a year ago is being able to predict from time zero how long this piece of work is going to take so that we can price it and still you know make sure that we're doing the work properly that we align with the value that we're giving the clients and you know that's like where things get really interesting because you have to predict you know how many times will this contract go back and forth.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels & John Sarihan (Crosby) — Sequoia Training Data Ep.61 · AI-native providers · 2026

qs.q: I think there are types of human labor that you can replace today but the amount that your clients will pay you may not be more than the inference costs  of serving those clients right just like that's just like raw raw raw math.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels — Crosby (AI-native law firm) · AI-native providers · 2025

kps.k: Partnership incentives and implementation capacity can constrain transformation even when lawyers find AI useful.
kps.d: Daniels argues that partners must sacrifice current distributions for uncertain returns, with senior decision-makers potentially having shorter investment horizons; he considers this more important than hourly billing alone. Walker calls for operational budgets, authority and partner leadership through short-term disruption. Ford recommends executive backing, small-group champions and patient client–firm investment, including tolerance for an initial productivity dip. Skoghag and the SRA panel favour defining and improving the process before choosing a tool, because some problems need no technology. These accounts challenge both the assumption that purchasing software delivers transformation and the stereotype that lawyers uniformly resist change.

qs.q: So if you have this like double incentive structure challenge which is one the partners need to vote on this capex thing and two our model is going to be changing and who the heck  knows it might take three or four or five years for that paper to be proven out but in the meantime maybe your revenue does shrink a little bit.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels — Crosby (AI-native law firm) · AI-native providers · 2025

qs.q: I think you have to start off with the groundwork and actually do the process mapping and see what can be improved with sort of the quick wins today before moving on to actually  finding a tool that's suiting the issue.
qs.a: Emelie Skoghag: How Legal Technologists Transform Law Firms · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: Firm-specific context, connected data and expert feedback underpin the proposed move from chat assistance to multi-step execution.
kps.d: Harvey describes reusable research and extraction components, matter-based agents and prospective firm-specific systems. Eudia stresses integration with existing enterprise data; Supio, GC AI and CoCounsel describe extending assistance across drafting, communication and surrounding workflows. The intended benefit is continuity: systems retain client context and reuse institutional knowledge rather than restart with each prompt. Pereyra argues that final documents omit the decisions and corrections needed to improve models. However, long-running agents, comprehensive transaction completion and bespoke systems at every firm remain partly research directions or roadmaps. Will Chen’s lean-build optimism also carries an enterprise-readiness qualification, while Wakeling recommends preserving vendor portability.

qs.q: So you have all of the context of a fund formation, an acquisition, a litigation, and the models are starting to learn, let me go in the document management system and see if I can find this, go in the data room or do case law research, get feedback from the partner.
qs.a: Gabe Pereyra — Harvey (No Priors Ep. 142) · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: And so uh you know kind of a lot of the work has actually been already connecting to a lot of those data sources internally because once you go beyond the pilot it really becomes critical that you actually do have a way to  >> this another way of looking at it  obviously is is that they don't actually have to nothing has to leave their building as it were.
qs.a: Omar Haroun — Eudia: Outcomes, the Law-Firm Arm, and the In-House Bet for 2026 · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Human oversight remains central, but its presence alone does not establish reliable legal outcomes.
kps.d: General Legal requires licensed-attorney oversight; Crosby retains expert quality judgments; Harvey envisages agents executing work under human review. Shaver argues that verification must examine reasoning, meaning and word choice, not just citations. Separately, Weinberg and Pereyra describe the difficulty of evaluating nuanced legal work and the usefulness of narrower tasks and realistic synthetic matters. These development practices are not substitutes for checking live output. Wakeling favours assessing errors against the existing workflow and use case rather than demanding abstract perfection. The discussion of lawyers reaching opposite defensible conclusions further qualifies claims that a single benchmark can capture legal judgment.

qs.q: All of the work that we do must be overseen by a licensed ~ attorney.
qs.a: Ryan Walker — General Legal: Rebuilding the Law Firm, the MSO Structure, and Supervision · AI-native providers · 2026

qs.q: When we use AI, even when you try really hard to apply your human judgment, you're you're verifying, but you may not necessarily be thinking, how can I abbreviate this or is this actually saying what I wanted it to say?
qs.a: Nikki Shaver — Legaltech Hub (agentic governance and the efficacy turn) · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: Observed uptake supports a case for practical usefulness, but does not establish firm-wide ROI or market transformation.
kps.d: Zuklie estimates daily use by about 60% of Orrick lawyers while explicitly describing assistance, not transformation. Berrent reports Covenant transaction self-service rising from 55% to 90%, with an expected 80% plateau, but gives no year or sample size. Daniels claims maintained two-hour contract turnaround without comparative performance evidence. These operating reports are more concrete than forecasts, yet do not independently demonstrate causation, accuracy or profitability. Pereyra locates emerging ROI stories in specialised client workflows; Legalweek commentators report continuing uncertainty about firm-wide returns. Practical measurement proposals separate turnaround, quality, human touchpoints and financial effects from adoption, morale and newly possible work.

qs.q: like a two-hour contract turnaround no matter what is is pretty crazy.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels — Crosby (AI-native law firm) · AI-native providers · 2025

qs.q: We're doing this with ANO, PWC, uh some other law firms we can't disclose, but I think a lot of it is localizing it to practice areas because I think the big challenge is when you use Harvey as a horizontal assistant, it's hard to map this to ROI.
qs.a: Gabe Pereyra — Harvey: 'the models are the product', ROI, and turning firm expertise into saleable models · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: The competitive outlook ranges from incumbent expansion to consolidation and AI-native entry, with important market-segment boundaries.
kps.d: Walker predicts an AmLaw reshuffle; Junestrand envisages substantial consolidation and particular pressure on mid-sized firms. Pereyra instead stresses the possibility of larger firms and the difficulty of replicating full-service capabilities with a few breakaway partners. Berrent targets the middle market while excluding the most bespoke high-end matters; Manifest OS focuses on process-heavy corporate immigration rather than Big Law generally. Devlin-Brown expects uneven adaptation but continuing demand for excellent firms. Thus, the debate concerns redistribution and differentiation as much as replacement. Brands, accumulated expertise, client relationships, capital and regulatory constraints remain relevant, and the supplied material does not demonstrate the predicted rankings changes.

qs.q: Well, so I I mean our belief is  that we're going to see a major shuffling of the AmLaw 200 in the next few years.
qs.a: Ryan Walker — General Legal: The Rise of AI-Native Law Firms and the AmLaw Reshuffle · AI-native providers · 2026

qs.q: So I think law firms will go through a quite significant consolidation period because so far there hasn't been a lot of um incentives to consolidate law firms but now actually private equity wants to get in on the action want to fund different law firms who want to become AI powered again coming back to the idea of do you want to own the whole stack or do you just want to work with the best service layer.
qs.a: Legora CEO, Max Junestrand: $7M ARR in a Day | Harvey vs Legora: Is a Legal AI Winner Takes All? · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Task displacement, project staffing and total employment are distinct claims, and speakers disagree about their relationship.
kps.d: Weinberg predicts fewer people per project but potentially more projects and larger firms. Ford, Logvinova and Marwaha expect faster business activity, regulatory complexity and neglected work to absorb released capacity. Junestrand nevertheless predicts fewer juniors for existing workloads and reports clients leaving vacancies unfilled while revenue rises; Berrent expects fewer paperwork-processing jobs. Robinson’s smaller boutique profession is a desired ten-year future, not an employment finding. These positions cannot establish the net labour effect: demand expansion, insourcing and task automation can occur together, and the evidence here consists mainly of forecasts, analogies and unquantified observations.

qs.q: >> I don't know if law firms are  necessarily going to get smaller because there's actually a world in which because AI allows you to institutionalize your knowledge faster and work across a a lot of different projects faster, you might actually be able to scale faster as a law firm than you used to be able to in the in the past, but you will need less people per project, right?
qs.a: Winston Weinberg — Harvey (CEO) on Judgment Versus Routine Work, Lockstep Promotion and Why Legal Fees Haven't Fallen · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: I do think that there will probably be less junior lawyers and trainees, but because I think that you just won't need as many people to execute the work that the firm has.
qs.a: Legora CEO, Max Junestrand: $7M ARR in a Day | Harvey vs Legora: Is a Legal AI Winner Takes All? · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Redesigning delivery also requires redesigning how lawyers acquire judgment, rather than assuming automation automatically improves training.
kps.d: Weinberg and Young favour earlier client responsibility; Ford’s Stefko Dover favours shadowing and residency-style learning over repetitive processing. Pereyra proposes firm-specific curricula and simulated matters for humans and agents. Against automatic acceleration, Wendy on the SRA panel stresses the internalised understanding gained through varied contract experience, while Klinger warns that insourcing removes mid- and senior-associate training work. Pereyra also recognises associate leverage’s role in identifying future partners. Proposed responses include deliberate supervision, varied experience, simulations and Klinger’s possible in-house-first career route, with greater teaching obligations for legal-department leaders. None has demonstrated equivalent or superior training outcomes in these excerpts.

qs.q: But that means basically we are doing the mid to senior level associate work enabled by technology that was the very work that trained young lawyers that that I trained on as a litigator that our deal lawyers trained on as young lawyers.
qs.a: Shannon Thyme Klinger — Moderna (Chief Legal Officer) on rewiring a legal function around AI · In-house counsel · 2025

qs.q: You could say, “I want to run a simulated fund formation, a simulated litigation, a simulated merger,” and go through the process end to end, getting feedback from a simulated client and simulated partners.
qs.a: Harvey's Gabe Pereyra on the Future of Legal AI · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: The proposed human role extends beyond strategy to accountability, relationships and building legal operations; broader access remains a separate, unproven benefit.
kps.d: Pereyra rejects a clean division between automated routine work and exclusively human strategy, and the Wordsmith exchange emphasises lawyers building persistent business workflows. Ziniti favours embedding lawyers in product teams; Poe treats client-serving technology development as legal work. Personal trust still matters in Covenant’s acquisition process, and Junestrand retains human accountability even with self-service delivery. Consumer-facing arguments are distinct: Browder targets small claims that lawyers rarely handle, while Young and the SRA panel preserve human support for consequential matters. Reported court projects and access ambitions do not establish reduced unmet civil legal need, and enterprise savings should not stand in for that evidence.

qs.q: I think the reality is with this technology is it's not going to be a binary split of like it's good at strategic, it's good at automating the lower level work.
qs.a: Gabe Pereyra — Harvey: agents as 'newspapers on the internet', training associates, and the bet on specialised firm systems · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: If the client has a legal problem that requires legal services from a law firm, and the work I'm doing is in direct service of solving that problem, that's legal work.
qs.a: E45 - How to Get a Job at Legora, Harvey and Other Legal AI Startups, Kyle Poe, VP of Legal Innovation at Legora · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an:
The curated AI-native-provider sources collectively accept the proposition that AI’s larger opportunity lies in redesigning legal delivery around repeatable services, rather than merely making individual lawyers faster. They materially extend it with concrete provider-side models: integrated lawyer–engineer teams at Crosby and Norm Law; software-first, direct-to-client delivery at Covenant; automation beneath experienced lawyers at General Legal; niche workflow redesign in corporate immigration and consumer rights; and aggregation of regulated firms around Lawhive’s proprietary AI platform. Common reasons include incumbent partnership and investment constraints, the need to redesign workflows from first principles, clients’ limited capacity to implement automation themselves, and the possibility of aligning delivery with document-based, flat-rate or other non-hourly pricing. Human oversight, embedded expertise and client trust remain central across most accounts.

Material variation concerns market segment, degree of substitution and commercial strategy. Some providers enable substantial client self-service or target work lawyers rarely serve; others retain experienced lawyers above an automated first pass. Some compete on speed, quality and integration rather than price, while others emphasise low-cost repeatable transactions. Several preserve hourly billing or bespoke traditional counsel for unpredictable, specialised or consequential matters. Claims of market reshuffling, technology-like margins, broad access gains and large-scale automation are mostly forecasts or ambitions. Reported uptake, turnaround and customer examples indicate practical usefulness but generally lack independent comparisons, measurement methods or evidence of firm-wide profitability and reliable outcomes. These sources therefore build out the proposition operationally without establishing that any one provider structure is generally superior or that market-wide transformation has already occurred.

qs.q: The reason why we incorporated our own law firm and have our lawyers who are using our product sitting next to our engineers is because we don't want AI to just be doing 10% of their workflow.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels — Crosby (AI-native law firm) · AI-native providers · 2025

qs.q: We believe that you need to go direct to clients and we believe that you need to embed legal expertise into the process um at different points.
qs.a: Jen Berrent — Covenant (founder) on what makes a firm 'AI-first' · AI-native providers · 2025

vlens.an:
The selected in-house counsel and legal-operations sources accept the cluster’s principal proposition that AI requires organisational redesign rather than merely accelerating individual lawyers. They materially extend it from the buyer side. Their common reasoning is that corporate legal departments increasingly value actionable decisions, risk assessment and expert judgment over document volume; can move some sophisticated drafting and workflow management in-house; and can use purchasing influence to reshape the allocation of work and collaboration with outside counsel. They also identify concrete redesign mechanisms: targeted outside review, technology-enabled client–firm workflows, agent platforms that package firm expertise into repeatable services, executive sponsorship, small-group champions and patient joint investment.

There is material variation within this shared direction. Klinger emphasises insourcing and its disruption of the traditional law-firm training pipeline, proposing collaborative training and a possible in-house-first career route. Vaughn and Stefko Dover place greater weight on higher-value problem-solving, adoption structures and residency-style development rather than preserving routine associate work. Anderson most directly develops the repeatable-services proposition by describing an emerging agent platform that monetises a firm’s people, expertise and client-derived value. Logvinova and Vaughn support redesign but are more cautious about commercial implications: they expect diversified delivery and value propositions without assuming the billable hour will disappear, and they stress that the industry is early in adoption. Across the sources, claimed benefits are primarily practitioner observations, recommendations and forecasts rather than comparative evidence of firm-wide ROI or proof that any operating model will prevail. These curated sources should not be treated as representative of all in-house counsel or legal-operations professionals.

qs.q: We do many more first drafts now even of sophisticated licensing agreements and then send them to our outside deal council and say can you please spend an hour on this and can you look at the following provisions that has been fantastic from an efficiency and cost savings perspective.
qs.a: Shannon Thyme Klinger — Moderna (Chief Legal Officer) on rewiring a legal function around AI · In-house counsel · 2025

qs.q: But they were trying to curate all of that into a monetizable agent platform.
qs.a: Inside Microsoft Legal: A Look at AI Use Built for Scale (Rebecca Anderson - Head of Legal EMEA Microsoft) · In-house counsel · 2026

vlens.an: These curated traditional-practice sources broadly accept the proposition that AI will change legal delivery, but they develop it from the incumbent law-firm perspective rather than assuming immediate conversion to AI-native, repeatable-service models. Their common reasoning is that stronger in-house capability and more sophisticated buying will force firms to demonstrate incremental value; firm data, persistent matter context and captured lawyer decision traces could make expertise more reusable; and AI can remove bounded administrative or first-level work while lawyers retain responsibility for judgment. Material variation concerns the maturity and extent of redesign. Zuklie redirects attention to gradual, bottom-up assistance and expressly says Orrick has not yet reached augmentation, automation or transformation. Devlin-Brown more directly supports changed workflows and buyer expectations but expects continuing demand for excellent firms and does not foresee the necessary disappearance of hourly billing. The Dhein discussion most clearly extends the organisational-redesign thesis by identifying decision traces as a mechanism for encoding collective expertise, while also stressing that legitimate disagreement between capable lawyers limits straightforward standardisation. The evidence is predominantly practitioner experience, reported conversations and forecasts rather than demonstrated firm-wide ROI or comparative proof that repeatable-service economics outperform traditional delivery.

qs.q: and he was saying that he felt that Harvey's moat wasn't just their distribution, the fact that lots of law firms are already using them, but also they captured what he called decision traces.
qs.a: Olivia Dhein: Lawyers, AI, And The New Non-Negotiable · Law firms · 2026

vlens.an:
Across this curated legal-tech-vendor voice, the sources accept the proposition that AI’s more consequential effect is organisational redesign rather than isolated lawyer productivity, and materially develop it with concrete delivery mechanisms. Common proposals include encoding firm expertise and client context into specialised systems; chaining reusable task components into matter-level or agentic workflows; enabling client self-service with human escalation; integrating legal AI with enterprise data and systems of record; unbundling work among in-house teams, law firms and ALSPs; and redesigning pricing, staffing and implementation around those workflows. Vendors also describe new professional roles—legal engineers, transformation teams and lawyers who build operational infrastructure—as necessary to convert software into repeatable delivery.

Material variation concerns where the redesigned work should sit. Harvey and Legora generally favour supplying software and implementation support to incumbent firms and legal departments, partly because combining a law firm and technology company creates a two-business execution burden. Other accounts place greater weight on in-house insourcing, integrated lawyer-plus-platform models, or AI-enabled independent boutiques. The sources also differ on labour effects: some predict fewer juniors or smaller project teams, others expect demand expansion, larger firms or unchanged professional headcount. A minority redirect attention toward augmentation, proactive advice or narrowly measurable document-analysis use cases rather than repeatable-service models, while several capability-focused excerpts do not address organisational redesign clearly.

The support is predominantly strategic and experiential rather than conclusive. Product architectures, implementation practices and selected adoption examples make the proposition more operationally specific, but firm-wide ROI, reliable end-to-end execution, employment effects and the relative performance of competing provider structures remain unsettled. Human verification, expert evaluation, data integration, enterprise trust and partnership incentives recur as constraints. This assessment characterises only the supplied curated sources and does not imply that all legal-tech vendors share the position.

This curated set of market-analysis, consultancy and press sources generally accepts the proposition that AI’s larger significance lies in redesigning legal delivery, not merely accelerating individual lawyers, and materially develops it with implementation and commercial detail. Common themes include mapping and improving processes before selecting technology; encoding firm expertise into specialised, client-facing systems; chaining reusable AI components into workflows; designing for vendor portability; moving technical optimisation away from lawyers; and applying substantive human verification to reasoning and meaning. The sources also connect redesign to hybrid pricing, buyer influence and continued demand for human capacity and expertise. Material variation concerns the preferred organisational form and expected effects: some emphasise bespoke technology within incumbent firms, others regard integrated AI-enabled service providers as the greater competitive challenge, while one Harvey interview remains focused on targeted task automation and partner development without clearly endorsing repeatable-service delivery. Claims about revenue, ROI, adoption, labour effects and market transformation are mostly forecasts, anecdotes or company-reported experience rather than comparative outcome evidence; the selected sources should not be treated as representative of all analysts, consultancies or press.

qs.q: I think you have to start off with the groundwork and actually do the process mapping and see what can be improved with sort of the quick wins today before moving on to actually  finding a tool that's suiting the issue.
qs.a: Emelie Skoghag: How Legal Technologists Transform Law Firms · Market & press · 2026

vlens.an: This curated set of regulators, professional-body participants and adjacent institutional voices accepts the cluster’s central proposition that AI’s significance lies in organisational redesign rather than isolated task acceleration, and materially extends it. The sources converge on converting institutional knowledge into repeatable workflows, moving toward multi-step agentic execution, and redesigning training so expertise can be retained and transmitted when routine work is automated. They also share a practical implementation logic: begin with defined problems, embed governance and human review, and treat adoption as organisational change rather than software procurement. Material variation concerns confidence and emphasis. The SRA panel supplies operational examples but stresses responsible deployment, context-sensitive boundaries and preservation of experiential learning; Pereyra proposes firm-specific training systems and simulated end-to-end matters, while acknowledging through the source framing that accelerated learning remains a prediction rather than a measured result; the Legalweek discussion is more cautious, supporting the need for redesign while observing that firm-wide ROI remains unclear. Thus, these sources develop concrete workflow, governance and training implications without demonstrating that the proposed models reliably produce superior outcomes, profitability or market-wide transformation. Their number should not be read as indicating how prevalent these views are among regulators, courts or professional bodies.

qs.q: You could say, “I want to run a simulated fund formation, a simulated litigation, a simulated merger,” and go through the process end to end, getting feedback from a simulated client and simulated partners.
qs.a: Harvey's Gabe Pereyra on the Future of Legal AI · Regulators & courts · 2026

elens.an:
The 2023–2024 sources collectively accept the proposition that generative AI’s more important effect may be redesigning legal delivery rather than merely accelerating individual lawyers, and they materially develop it with early operating principles. Across this curated set, the common logic is that value comes from reorganising work into specialised assistants, reliable workflows, repeatable consumer services and more decision-oriented in-house delivery. The sources add concrete requirements: workflow design and structured data; routing tasks among models to control inference costs; enterprise data protections and trust; use-case-specific risk assessment; vendor portability; executive sponsorship, small-group champions and patient client–firm collaboration; and changes to lawyer training and value propositions.

There is material internal variation in the envisioned model. Robinson favours specialised legal AI and aspires to a smaller, AI-supported profession, but does not demonstrate displacement. Browder describes an AI-enabled consumer-rights service for small unmet claims while resisting substitution in serious criminal and emotionally complex matters. Ford’s in-house speakers expect greater legal demand and redirect value from document production toward actionable advice, rather than predicting fewer lawyers. Boehmig emphasises embedding AI selectively in established contract workflows rather than autonomous legal delivery, while Wakeling focuses on products around language models, use-case risk and portability. Logvinova and Vaughn similarly anticipate reinvesting saved capacity in expert judgment and new delivery methods without expecting the billable hour simply to disappear.

Thus, the period builds on the proposition by supplying practical organisational mechanisms and boundary conditions, not by proving industry-wide transformation. The evidence is chiefly practitioner experience, product accounts, recommendations and forecasts; it does not establish comparative organisational performance, reliable legal outcomes, firm-wide ROI, lower prices, broader access to justice or net employment effects.

The curated 2025 sources collectively accept the proposition that AI’s more consequential effect comes from redesigning legal delivery around repeatable services, not merely accelerating individual lawyers, and materially develop it with concrete organisational models. They describe firms encoding expertise into specialised client-facing systems, AI-native providers colocating lawyers and engineers to automate deeper portions of workflows, and in-house teams insourcing drafting or institutionalising knowledge through multi-step agents. Common reasons include scaling expertise beyond associate headcount, preserving client context across matters, connecting AI to established workflows and data, and aligning efficiency with fixed-fee or hybrid pricing. Material variation concerns who should deliver the work: software vendors partnering with incumbent firms, integrated AI-native providers, stronger in-house teams, or AI-enabled boutiques. Sources also differ on the pace and extent of change: some describe emerging workflow and self-service practices, while others emphasise incremental assistance, continuing human capacity, bespoke high-end work and unresolved training needs. Partnership financing, implementation capacity, evaluation difficulty, inference costs and hourly-billing incentives are recurring constraints. The evidence is therefore strongest as a set of operating examples, strategic mechanisms and forecasts; it does not establish firm-wide ROI, reliable end-to-end autonomy or market-wide transformation. The source count should not be read as prevalence because the corpus is curated rather than a survey.

elens.an:
The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the principal proposition and materially develop it with concrete operating models rather than treating AI chiefly as an individual copilot. They describe repeatable delivery through firm-specific systems, reusable workflows, client self-service, integrated data, first-pass AI, lawyer–engineer teams, and AI-enabled in-house operations. Common reasons are that organisational redesign can preserve and reuse institutional knowledge and client context, allocate work more selectively, remove routine production from lawyers’ bills, and align delivery with buyer outcomes. Human verification, accountability and relationship-based trust generally remain integral rather than optional.

Material internal variation concerns who should control delivery and how value should be captured. AI-native providers such as Crosby, General Legal, Norm Law, Covenant, Soxton and Lawhive favour integrating technology with legal-service operations; Junestrand instead prefers vendors to equip incumbent firms rather than own both software and service layers. Other sources emphasise stronger in-house teams, selective unbundling among firms and ALSPs, or incumbent firms packaging expertise into bespoke systems. Pricing proposals range from fixed or per-document fees to hybrid models that retain hourly billing for unpredictable specialist work. Labour forecasts also diverge between fewer juniors or staff per matter and demand expansion that could sustain or enlarge firms.

The evidence remains substantially more developed as organisational theory and implementation practice than as proof of outcomes. Sources report operating examples, adoption and some company-specific claims, but many assertions about margins, spending reductions, consolidation, training and market reshuffling are forecasts or unquantified observations. One source redirects attention toward narrowly defined augmentation and measurable document-analysis value, while another does not address organisational redesign directly; these qualifications do not displace the period’s overall constructive extension of the proposition.

qs.q: But I think that, like, my decision to leave is, I think half of what needs to be disrupted here is the business model.
